paras: The threats against the Blackville Republican meeting were published calls in July 1880 by Democratic newspapers in Barnwell County, South Carolina, for Democratic clubs to attend a Republican ratification meeting at Blackville, which Republican papers read as a summons to break it up. The meeting, held on July 27, was later reported to have drawn more than 4,000 people and to have passed without disturbance. Northern Republican papers nonetheless cited the episode as evidence of "bulldozing" in the 1880 campaign, while Democratic papers used its peaceful outcome to ridicule those warnings.

The Republicans of Barnwell County called a meeting at Blackville for Tuesday, July 27, 1880, to ratify the nomination of Garfield and Arthur, with E. W. M. Mackey and W. N. Taft advertised as speakers. Republican writers recalled that the county included Ellenton, where, in the words of a New York Times correspondent, the Red Shirt, rifle and sabre clubs had "committed the outrage and murder in 1876."

Two Barnwell papers responded to the announcement by summoning Democrats to the meeting. The People called Mackey and Taft "the bravest and most brazen Radicals in the State," declared that the Democrats would hold the state "at every hazard," and said it had been asked "by the highest competent Democratic authority" to invite all Democratic candidates to attend. The Barnwell Sentinel urged that "all clubs send fair representatives" made up of men "who will nail lies to the wall as fast as they are told."

Writing from Charleston on July 24, the New York Times correspondent predicted that the clubs would take over the platform, invite Democratic speakers and order the Republicans to step off, while Mackey and Taft said they meant to be heard even if they had to sacrifice their lives. The only description of the meeting itself comes from a satirical Detroit Free Press item, which said more than 4,000 "colored Republicans" attended and that Democrats were present "in great numbers" but listened without jeering or interrupting.

No report of violence, arrests or injuries at the meeting appears in the coverage. In September the Boston Herald, an independent paper, wrote that after "the great meeting at Blackville" was not disturbed, Republican organs shifted their complaint from suppressed debate to cheating in the count.

All of the coverage found came from white papers, most of it Northern Republican editorials that quoted the Barnwell papers as proof of Democratic intimidation. The New York Times dispatch ran in Michigan and, under the headline "South Carolina Bull-Dozers Under Orders," in Ohio, and the Boston Advertiser concluded that the language had "but one meaning," that the meeting "must be broken up." The Sacramento Record-Union called the Sentinel's notice "a call for the rifle clubs to attend and break up the meeting," and a Pennsylvania editorial reprinted in Portland, Maine, glossed "attended" as "broken up."

Democratic papers answered with ridicule after the fact. The Detroit Free Press piece, reprinted in Missouri, mocked Republicans for wanting "a Democratic mob" to supply the "Northern outrage market," and the Tallahassee Weekly Floridian reprinted the Herald's remark that the meeting had gone undisturbed. No Black-press coverage of the meeting was found.

Accounts differ on what the calls meant rather than on any act: Republican papers, writing before or on the day of the meeting, treated them as a threat to break it up, while the only later reports, from Democratic-leaning and independent papers, said Democrats attended peacefully. No Republican or eyewitness account of the meeting itself appears in the coverage.

reader.title: Threats against the Blackville Republican meeting (1880)
bases: Democratic papers in Barnwell County urged party clubs to attend a Republican meeting, which Republican papers read as a threat to break it up (A2, A5, A9); no violence at the meeting was reported (A8, A10).

The Barnwell papers' calls are quoted alike in several reports (A2, A5, A9), but their reading as a threat is a Republican interpretation, and two Democratic-leaning reports say the meeting went off undisturbed (A8, A10).

accounts.label: N.Y. Times Charleston correspondent
accounts.gist: Before the meeting, predicted that the Red Shirt, rifle and sabre clubs would attend, take over the platform and turn it into a Democratic 'pow-wow'.

accounts.label: Republican editorials (Boston Advertiser, Sacramento Record-Union, Penn. Weekly Notes)
accounts.gist: Read the Barnwell papers' language as having one meaning, that the meeting must be broken up, and as evidence of bulldozing in the campaign.

accounts.label: Detroit Free Press (satire)
accounts.gist: Said over 4,000 attended a meeting of colored Republicans and the Democrats present listened without jeering or interrupting.

accounts.label: Boston Herald
accounts.gist: Said that the great meeting at Blackville was not disturbed, after Republican papers had predicted it would not be permitted.

framing.detail: Republican papers headlined the item 'South Carolina Bull-Dozers Under Orders' and 'The Ballot at the South', recalling the 1876 Ellenton killings and calling it bulldozing.
The Detroit Free Press mocked Republicans for hoping for a 'Northern outrage market' and praised the Democrats' restraint at Blackville.
The independent Boston Herald, quoted by a Florida Democratic weekly, cited the undisturbed meeting to dispute claims that free debate was impossible in the South.

versions.value: Republican papers expected the meeting to be taken over or broken up by Democratic clubs
The meeting was held and not disturbed; Democrats attended but did not interrupt

conflicts.note: The Republican reports were written before or on the day of the meeting and describe expectations; the two later reports of a peaceful meeting are from a satirical Democratic item and an independent paper. No Republican or eyewitness account of the meeting itself was found.
